opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underappreciated dynamics. People often picture AI progress as a smooth curve: each model is a bit better than the last, so the impact on the world should grow a bit at a time. But impact doesn't depend only on the model. It depends on the model plus everything it's plugged into.

The analogy I find useful is something like electricity or the internet. Once the infrastructure is in place, meaning the APIs, the integrations, the agent scaffolding, the tool access, the habits people have built around delegating tasks, then a capability improvement doesn't have to build its own path to the world. It inherits the path. So a model that crosses some threshold, say it can reliably complete a multi-step task instead of failing a third of the time, could go from basically useless in a workflow to basically indispensable almost overnight. The workflow was already there, waiting.

That threshold-crossing matters because a lot of usefulness is quite nonlinear in reliability. If an agent succeeds 70% of the time, you still have to check everything, so it's not saving you much. At 98%, suddenly you can actually hand things off. The underlying improvement might look modest on a benchmark, but in deployment it's a phase change.

There's also a sense in which we're building up a kind of overhang. Every company that wires AI into its systems, every developer who builds tooling expecting the models to get better, adds latent capacity. Each new model gets dropped into a richer environment than the last one did. So even if model progress were perfectly steady, I'd expect the curve of real-world impact to be lumpier and possibly steeper.

I'm uncertain about how big these jumps would be in practice. There are real frictions: organizations are slow, people don't trust new systems, regulation, liability, all of that. Those can smooth things out a lot. But I think the frictions are mostly about adopting the infrastructure in the first place. Once it's adopted, swapping in a better model is close to frictionless. That's the part that makes me think step changes are quite plausible, and it's part of why I think it's worth paying attention not just to model capabilities but to how much of the world is already set up to amplify them.

r001.rationale: The response describes existing AI infrastructure that can amplify model capabilities, but does not identify this as a difference from almost every other technology.

r002.rationale: It says developers build tools expecting models to improve, but does not explain that this expectation makes them willing to tolerate complements that currently do not work.

r003.rationale: It describes threshold effects and potentially lumpy impact, but does not suggest that many previously built complements could activate at once with unpredictable consequences.

r004.rationale: Electricity and the internet appear as infrastructure analogies; the response does not question AI’s distinctiveness by comparing model updates with updates to other widely deployed technologies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the more important and underappreciated dynamics. When people imagine AI progress, they often picture the model itself getting smarter as the main driver, and the model does matter a lot. But the thing that determines how much a given level of capability actually changes the world is everything around it: the APIs, the tooling, the integrations with email and browsers and code repositories, the companies whose entire workflows are already built around calling a model, the people who've learned how to prompt and delegate.

And that infrastructure has been accumulating steadily, mostly in response to models that weren't quite good enough to use it fully. So you get this situation where a lot of latent capacity is sitting there, waiting. Agent frameworks that mostly fail, but would work if the model were a bit more reliable. Automated pipelines where a human still has to check every step. The scaffolding has been built ahead of the thing it's scaffolding for.

What that means is that a model improvement that looks fairly incremental on benchmarks could have a quite discontinuous effect in practice. You cross some threshold of reliability, and suddenly all of those half-working systems start working, roughly at once, because they're all plugged into the same model behind the same API. You don't have to build the distribution channels after the fact. The new model just gets dropped into millions of existing deployments, often within days.

I think this is a bit different from historical technologies, where even a big capability jump was bottlenecked by adoption. Electricity took decades partly because factories had to be redesigned. Here the redesign has been happening in advance, and in a fairly centralized way, so the lag between "capability exists" and "capability is deployed everywhere" could be very short.

The thing I'd flag as concerning about that is less the step change itself and more that it undermines our ability to respond gradually. A lot of our implicit safety story relies on noticing problems as they emerge and adjusting. If the impact arrives as a step rather than a slope, there's less time to notice. So I'd want people to pay attention not just to how good models are getting, but to how much enabling infrastructure is in place and how quickly a new model propagates through it. That ratio seems like a reasonable proxy for how surprised we might be.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI’s existing APIs, integrations, and deployments as infrastructure that could let a new model spread quickly, contrasting this with other historical technologies.

r002.rationale: It says complements are already being built despite models not yet being good enough, but does not explain that expectations of future upgrades make people willing to tolerate them.

r003.rationale: It says crossing a reliability threshold could make many half-working systems work roughly at once, and warns that the resulting rapid impact leaves less time to notice and respond.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts AI with electricity’s slow adoption; it does not suggest that updates to other widely deployed technologies offer analogous cases.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a reason to be cautious about extrapolating from the impact we’ve seen so far. A model doesn’t have to build all of the infrastructure for acting in the world itself. There are already computers, the internet, ways of paying for things, and people you can communicate with. If a new model becomes capable of using those things effectively, then a lot of possibilities could open up fairly quickly.

You could have a gradual improvement in the underlying capability, but a much less gradual change in what it’s useful for. If a system can almost reliably carry out some long task, perhaps you still need a person supervising it, and that limits how much you can delegate. Once it can do the task reliably enough, you might be able to run many copies with much less supervision. That seems like a potentially important threshold.

I don’t think that establishes that there will be a sudden jump. There could be all sorts of practical bottlenecks. But it does make me less reassured by the observation that the previous model didn’t have a very large impact. The question is partly how close it was to being able to make use of a lot of things that are already there.

r001.rationale: It names existing computers, the internet, payment systems, and communication channels, but does not identify AI’s existing distribution infrastructure as a difference from almost every other technology.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss expectations of future model upgrades or people tolerating complements that currently do not work.

r003.rationale: It says effective use of existing infrastructure could open possibilities quickly, but does not describe many previously built AI complements activating at once or the consequences as unpredictable.

r004.rationale: It does not compare AI model updates with updates to other widely deployed technologies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real possibility. You can have a lot of gradual progress in the infrastructure around AI, and then a new model makes that infrastructure much more useful all at once. So even if the model itself represents a fairly incremental improvement, the effect on the world could be much larger.

For example, you might already have software that lets an AI interact with a computer and carry out tasks, but it needs enough supervision that it isn’t worth using for many things. Then a model gets sufficiently reliable, and suddenly you can leave it working on those tasks. You haven’t had to build a whole new system around it; a lot of the complementary pieces were waiting there.

I’d distinguish that from the claim that we should expect a particular, very large jump. There are still questions about which bottlenecks the model removes and which remain—whether people trust it, whether it can recover from mistakes, whether deploying it requires changes in an organization. But I don’t think smooth progress in model capabilities gives us much assurance of smooth progress in impact. The interaction with everything that’s already in place seems pretty important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing AI infrastructure and complementary pieces, but does not identify distribution infrastructure or compare AI with almost every other technology.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure may become more useful when models improve, but does not say that expectations of future upgrades make people tolerate complements that currently do not work.

r003.rationale: It describes a model making existing infrastructure suddenly useful, but does not clearly suggest that activating many built complements could have unpredictable consequences.

r004.rationale: The response does not question AI’s distinctiveness by comparing it with updates to other widely deployed technologies.
